contradiction.viewer_thinks: you are skating on solid ice
contradiction.actually: you glide on a microscopic quasi-liquid water film on the ice surface

beats.narration: You can stand on a frozen lake, yet glide across it like glass. Why is ice slippery?
beats.claim: ice is slippery because of a thin near-surface water layer, not standing water
beats.visual_question: why is ice slippery at all?
beats.visual_answer: a skate blade resting on bare ice, the slipperiness not yet explained

beats.narration: The classic answer blames pressure: the skate presses down, and the ice beneath it melts.
beats.claim: the textbook explanation attributes ice slipperiness to pressure melting under the blade
beats.visual_question: does a skate really melt the ice by pressing on it?
beats.visual_answer: a heavy downward pressure arrow squeezing meltwater out of the ice

beats.narration: Run the physics and pressure barely matters. A skater's weight lowers the melting point by only a fraction of a degree.
beats.claim: a skater's pressure lowers ice's melting point by only a fraction of a degree, far too little to make the water film
beats.visual_question: how much melting can that pressure actually buy?
beats.visual_answer: pressure lowers the melting point only a fraction of a degree: far too little

beats.narration: The real story starts at the surface. Even below freezing, ice wears a thin skin of water: a quasi-liquid layer.
beats.claim: a quasi-liquid layer exists on the ice surface even below the melting point
beats.visual_question: where does the water come from if no one is pressing?
beats.visual_answer: the bare ice surface carries its own quasi-liquid layer of water below freezing

beats.narration: Then glide adds heat. Friction between blade and ice warms that skin, feeding the water film faster than it can refreeze.
beats.claim: frictional heating during glide feeds the near-surface water film
beats.visual_question: what keeps the film flowing while the blade moves?
beats.visual_answer: friction heat from the gliding blade feeds the water film as it flows

beats.narration: But the film tends to thin as it gets colder. A blade that glides at minus five bites hard at minus thirty.
beats.claim: the quasi-liquid film thins as temperature falls, so blade behavior changes with cold
beats.visual_question: why does the same blade behave differently in deep cold?
beats.visual_answer: in deep cold the water film thins and the blade bites instead of gliding

beats.narration: The current picture: ice is slippery because it is already wet — a whisper of water, born at the surface, renewed under every glide.
beats.claim: ice's slipperiness comes from the ever-present near-surface water film, renewed by pressure, friction and cold-dependent thickness
beats.visual_answer: ice is already wet: a whisper of surface water, renewed under every glide

visual_contradiction.actually: a microscopic interface of quasi-liquid water underneath
visual_contradiction.reveal: the camera enters the ice surface and the hidden lubricating layer becomes visible

payoff_image.image: the skate blade riding its own invisible water film — solid above, liquid below, one frame holds the whole mechanism
